This research examines a controlled stochastic partial differential equation with non-compact support, where the state is driven by a stochastic gradient system and the control is restricted to a closed and bounded set. We investigate the existence and uniqueness of solutions for this control issue, as well as the convergence of its approximations. Additionally, we explore the random dynamics and establish the existence of a compact invariant set that is invariant under the control system. These findings are demonstrated through a specific example involving the controlled stochastic Cahn-Hilliard system. We also discuss the connection between the discrete and continuous solutions using the method of duality. Furthermore, we examine the random dynamics of the approximate solutions and show that they converge to the same invariant dynamics as the continuous solutions. These results were previously unknown and are the main innovation of this research. We believe these findings are significant additions to the field of stochastic partial differential equation control. Our comprehensive anisotropy analysis of extremely high-energy cosmic rays is presented, covering over 8 years of data and over 61,000 events with energies above 4 EeV. Utilizing a sophisticated method that accounts for local and galactic influences, we detected significant anisotropy patterns at the 10^-3 level in the all-sky distribution. A prominent dipole anisotropy of (6.4±0.9(stat)±0.9(sys)) x 10^-3) was found, pointing towards a cosmic-ray source direction towards right ascension 245.7°±1.4°±3.5° and declination 48.2°±1.1°±2.5°. Additionally, localized anisotropies of (5.1±0.7(stat)±0.7(sys)) x 10^-3) were observed in the direction of Centaurus, (3.8±0.7(stat)±0.7(sys)) x 10^-3) towards Scorpius, and (3.5±0.6(stat)±0.6(sys)) x 10^-3) towards Carina, along with indications of periodic anisotropies possibly linked to the Local Standard of Rest or the Galactic rotation. Furthermore, large-scale multipole anisotropies revealed patterns resembling the distribution of galaxies within the observable universe, with significant dipole and quadrupole components oriented towards the Cepheus void and the Shapley Supercluster respectively. The complex anisotropy picture presented here underscores the highly directional nature of cosmic-ray acceleration and/or emission. The observed anisotropies also suggest that our observable universe may contain numerous sources of extremely high-energy cosmic rays, with the most prominent ones located towards the Cepheus void, the Shapley Supercluster, the Centaurus cluster, the Scorpius cluster, the Carina-Sagittarius arm, and the Local Bubble. The extensive anisotropy coverage and the rich detail of the patterns presented here will serve as a foundation for future studies of the highest-energy universe. The task of integrating data tables involves fusing two tables, possibly with functional relationships, into a single, merged table. This integration process requires considering three types of relationships between tables: inner joins for two tables with no missing values, natural joins for two tables with no specified relationships, and functional relationships, which indicate that one table's values are completely determined by another table's values. In this research, we develop algorithms for integrating data tables with these three types of relationships in order to compare their structures and contents. Specifically, we created methods for identifying discrepancies between integrated tables and those that have been corrected for certain discrepancies. Furthermore, we established the computational time required for these integration tasks can be guaranteed to increase slowly with the size of input tables. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we applied it to real-world datasets and observed its performance to be several orders of magnitude better than existing methods. To facilitate experimentation with existing datasets, we made our integration tool available online. This research was presented at the 2020 ACM Conference on Management of Emergent Data Products.

A common and challenging issue arises when trying to recover sparse vectors using linear measurements that are contaminated with random errors. A promising approach involves using a specific method called $\ell_1$-regularized least squares, also known as LARS or the Lasso, which is known to accurately recover sparse signals under certain conditions. However, when the measurements are corrupted, the performance of this method degrades significantly. In recent years, researchers have proposed using a variant of the Lasso called the Damped Lasso, which involves a soft thresholding step in addition to the standard Lasso. This variant has been shown to recover sparse signals in the presence of random errors. In this work, we investigate the Damped Lasso and its variants, including the Iterated Damped Lasso, and the Multiresolution Damped Lasso. We examine the conditions under which these methods recover sparse signals and provide numerical examples demonstrating their performance in recovering sparse signals in various dimensions. We also propose a new measure called the Resolution Depth, which characterizes the recovery performance of these methods and provides a roadmap for recovering sparse signals based on the available data and desired level of precision. We also examine the recovery performance of these methods in recovering sparse signals in different dimensions and provide a numerical example of recovering a sparse signal in a high-dimensional space. We believe that our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the Damped Lasso and its variants and offers a roadmap for recovering sparse signals in various settings. The uncertainty associated with aerosol quantities poses a significant obstacle in retrieving accurate cloud optical properties from photometric measurements in the Earth. This issue is particularly pronounced in regions far from the equator. To overcome this challenge, researchers have traditionally relied on empirical models based on limited satellite data, but these methods have notable limitations. This study presents a new approach using machine learning models to estimate aerosol quantities directly from photometric measurements in the Earth, without intermediate assumptions about radiative transfer. This method, known as the "forward machine learning approach," enables the retrieval of aerosol quantities from photometric measurements in previously uncharted regions of the Earth. A comparative analysis of the forward and inverse machine learning approaches suggests that the former yields more accurate results in areas with limited satellite data, but also carries a higher computational cost. To further improve the accuracy of aerosol quantity estimates, this study proposes a hybrid model that incorporates additional satellite data and cloud properties. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of the forward machine learning approach in enhancing the accuracy of aerosol quantity estimates in previously uncharted regions of the Earth. This method can be applied to other satellite retrievals, such as cloud and aerosol properties, by leveraging machine learning models trained on high-resolution radiative transfer simulations. This study also presents a new dataset of photometric measurements in the Earth, along with the corresponding aerosol quantities and cloud properties, which can be utilized for training and validation purposes. To accurately simulate complex biomolecular systems, it is crucial to efficiently sample various configurational states. This is particularly important for modeling temperature fluctuations, given that thermal motions can significantly influence the behavior of molecules. However, certain sampling methods, such as molecular dynamics using the Langevin equation, are not well-suited for simulating large biomolecules due to their inherent bias towards equilibrium states and the limited range of temperature fluctuations they can accurately capture. This issue is compounded by the presence of hydrodynamic interactions, which can lead to slow diffusion rates and make it even more challenging to simulate large systems. This study introduces a novel algorithm, the "hybrid Langevin" method, which modifies the Langevin dynamics equation to remove temperature fluctuations' impact on dynamics while preserving the conservation of detailed balance. This modification enables efficient rejection sampling of configurations, even in systems with slow diffusion rates. By leveraging this algorithm, we demonstrate a significant improvement in sampling efficiency, with a 10-fold increase in accepted steps for a specific protein folding simulation. This improvement is particularly notable for systems with slow diffusion rates, where traditional rejection sampling methods often struggle to enhance sampling efficiency. This algorithm is particularly well-suited for modeling temperature fluctuations in systems with slow diffusion rates, such as protein folding during thermal denaturation, and can be applied to a wide range of biomolecular simulations, including simulations with hydrodynamic interactions and temperature fluctuations. A novel automated approach is proposed to segment neoplasms from CT scans of the esophagus using a modified Dense Focus Unet structure, dubbed DDAUnet. This model leverages a unique combination of spatial pyramid pooling and dilated convolutional layers to enhance feature extraction, and a separate refinement network to improve segmentation accuracy. To improve training efficiency, a class-weighted cross-entropy loss function is employed, along with a validation-based early stopping criterion to prevent overfitting. Evaluations using two publicly available datasets demonstrate the efficacy of DDAUnet, with a 94.5% Dice similarity coefficient and 85.6% average surface distance in the MINDO dataset, and a 94.1% DSC and 84.5% ASD in the Med-CYTE dataset. Compared to a standard Dense Unet, the proposed method shows a 3.5% relative improvement in DSC and 6.5% in ASD in the MINDO dataset, and a 2.5% DSC and 5% ASD in the Med-CYTE dataset. The proposed method exhibits a 2.5 fold reduction in training time and 1.5 fold reduction in inference time compared to the Dense Unet. Multilingual individuals can understand and produce code-mixed language, which blends two or more languages within a sentence. While this ability is beneficial for many linguistically diverse populations, it also presents challenges in understanding and generating language. Current NLP models often struggle with code-mixed data due to several issues. Firstly, code-mixed data lacks a standardized form, making it difficult to process. Secondly, the blending of languages can lead to multiple possible equivalent forms, making it hard to determine a singular representation. Thirdly, code-mixed data often contains a mix of formal and informal elements from different languages, which can make it difficult to model. Finally, the lack of large, publicly available datasets hinders the development of more sophisticated models. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a new approach to modeling code-mixed data by treating each word as a factor that combines multiple underlying elements. This method enables the model to capture complex relationships between words and handle the variability inherent in code-mixed data. To evaluate this approach, we developed a dataset for the task of code-mixed word retrieval, and our results show that this method outperforms a strong baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/kuangrujia/factor-code-mixing.

The primary objective of automatic image description generation is to provide accessible and searchable visual content for the visually impaired. Despite significant advancements in this field, the current methods are not perfect and often yield descriptions that are uninformative, inaccurate, or incomplete. As a result, there's a growing interest in utilizing human reference descriptions, which are considered ideal, to fine-tune and assess the quality of generated descriptions. In this research, we explore two key aspects of image description assessment using human references. Firstly, we evaluate the existing metrics to determine their effectiveness in evaluating the similarity between generated descriptions and human references. Our analysis reveals that the existing metrics are not sufficient to capture the nuances of human descriptions and provide a simple yet robust instruction that can be used to select the most suitable metric. Secondly, we investigate the correlation between the similarity scores obtained from human evaluation and those from the selected metric. Our findings indicate that there's a significant disparity between the two, which can be attributed to the inherent variability of human descriptions. To address this issue, we propose a simple yet effective approach to rectify the incompleteness and promote similarity in human descriptions prior to assessing the generated descriptions. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields a more uniform distribution of human descriptions and a higher correlation between the human evaluation and the selected metric. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for assessing the quality of generated descriptions using human references, which can be applied to the task of image description assessment. Tantalum oxide Ta$_2$O$_5$ is a highly complex and intriguing material with multiple possible crystal structures for its ground state, making it a prime subject for investigation. Using ab-initio calculations, a stable Ta$_{0.5}$Ta$_{0.5}$ dimer is consistently found across various experimental conditions, but the overall crystal structure remains uncertain due to conflicting results from different methods. To further explore the potential energy landscape, additional ab-initio and Monte Carlo simulations were conducted to map out the energy profiles and identify potential energy barriers. These findings highlight the difficulties in predicting the ground state of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and emphasize the importance of considering the role of local Ta-Ta dimer formation in transition metal oxides. Moreover, this study highlights the utility of combining ab-initio and Monte Carlo simulations to uncover the crystal structure and phase transitions of these complex materials. Lastly, possible experimental probes of Ta$_2$O$_5$'s crystal structure are proposed.

Humans use various sounds when interacting with robots, including beeps and speech. Studies have focused on audio feedback from robots but less attention has been given to the sounds made by humans while teaching robots. To better understand human-robot teaching, this research examines how humans produce sounds while demonstrating tasks to robots. We analyzed the types of sounds made by humans during these interactions and how they are affected by different teaching methods. Specifically, we explored the connection between human utterances and their corresponding actions in three domains: using the left hand, using the right hand, and combining both. Our findings reveal that humans use distinct sounds to indicate the use of either hand and that these sounds change based on the robot's action in response to the instruction. Notably, humans often use the same sound for the same action even after the robot has made a mistake, suggesting a level of expectation about the robot's behavior. These discoveries can be applied to improve the design of human-robot interfaces by incorporating sounds that reflect the robot's perceived actions and its anticipated future behavior. To facilitate this, we propose a method for mapping human utterances to intended actions and their associated probabilities. This research can be extended by examining the impact of different sounds on robot behavior through reinforcement learning and exploring the benefits of speech over other human sounds in the teaching process. Cross-domain recommendation has gained significant attention in recent years, especially in addressing the issue of limited data. A major challenge in this field is the scarcity of domain interconnection information, which hinders the effectiveness of current methods. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation via Improved Thorough Aspect Preference Learning (MSDCoR). This method assumes that users' preferences are represented by multiple sparse aspects, which are then aggregated to represent their comprehensive preferences. We introduce an attention-based mechanism to identify the most critical aspects for each user and employ a collaborative filtering model to capture the relationships between aspects and items. Furthermore, we develop an adaptive sampling strategy to select representative domains for inter-domain learning and utilize meta-learning to adapt to new domains. Optimizing conic programs over semirings using interior point methods can be challenging due to the need for precise ring operations. This limitation makes it difficult to solve high-dimensional organic conic formulations, which often arise in data applications. The accuracy of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial for medical diagnosis, and its assurance is a critical concern. In cerebral MRI, various factors such as hardware, operating systems, and individual differences can lead to image quality degradation. As MRI data are extensive and diverse, learning from pre-trained models has become a popular approach to quality assessment. However, the limited training data available for MRI is a significant challenge. In this work, we explore cerebral MRI quality assessment as a multidimensional generalization issue and present a novel framework to tackle this challenge. First, we train a quality prediction model using a small dataset from a specific MRI protocol. Then, we extend this model to new protocols by leveraging the intrinsic relationships between different MRI sequences. Furthermore, we introduce a transfer learning approach to generalize to new scanning parameters and individual differences. Experimental results on a large dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, showing significant improvements over baseline models. As a result, our framework can efficiently construct a quality assessment model for an unseen protocol or individual, with only 1000 new samples required. To analyze the impact of private electric vehicles on urban power resilience, a new decision-making framework is proposed that considers multiple objectives and uncertainty, using a multi-agent optimization approach with a private EV owner model and a city-scale model. First, a stochastic mixed-integer linear model is developed to represent private EV charging decisions, and another mixed-integer linear model is developed to represent municipal microgrid operations. Then, multi-objective optimization is performed to minimize costs and maximize resilience in municipal microgrid operations, using the private EV charging models as inputs. Finally, case studies in two cities demonstrate the effects of private EVs on municipal microgrid resilience, and show that private EVs can enhance resilience in certain scenarios, but may also exacerbate inequality among urban residents. Additionally, scenarios with increased private EV adoption show that public policy support may be necessary to ensure equitable access to urban power resilience. Finally, opportunities for future research are discussed. This work is the first to investigate the impact of private EVs on municipal microgrid resilience using data from actual cities, and provides a practical framework for evaluating the effects of private EVs on urban power resilience that can be applied to other cities. In multi-agent dialogue research, assessing the effectiveness of agents in collaborative conversations has traditionally been challenging due to the diverse and often unclear objectives. To address this issue, researchers have started using game frameworks, particularly those based on partial reward methods, which provide a flexible and quantifiable evaluation metric. In this work, we present a Mass Game theory-inspired approach to assign individual rewards to agents within a dialogue task, which facilitates statistical optimization to improve the overall dialogue performance. To demonstrate the versatility of this method, we created a simple dialogue scenario involving two agents working together to solve a mystery. In this example, we assigned a unique objective to each agent, which was reflected in their individual rewards. As a result, our analysis showed that by optimizing their own rewards, each agent was able to contribute effectively to the joint problem-solving, and together they were able to solve the mystery in a relatively small number of turns. In contrast to traditional evaluation methods, this approach enables the exploration of complex performance in controlled environments, as evidenced by the diverse solutions found in our experiments. Our code is available online at: https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/MRMID.

The foundation theorem is a significant concept originating from graph theory, which has been successfully applied to Coxeter systems of type B. This leading principle provides an inclusive framework for the properties and structures of finite Coxeter systems of type B, notably revealing the connection between the Coxeter element's order and the system's characteristics. In expanding upon previous research, we demonstrate how the foundation theorem's implications extend to infinite Coxeter systems of type B, thereby solidifying its generality and utility in infinite settings. Furthermore, we derive an inequality that links the order of a Coxeter element to the product of localized system parameters, and in the context of finite systems, this inequality takes on a more precise form that directly relates the order to the product of system parameters. This in turn offers an explicit expression for the order of a Coxeter element, which in the case of finite systems reduces to a known formula following a different derivation path. This research on the foundation theorem for Coxeter systems of type B also explores the concept of minimal support, and provides a characterization of the support of a given order, which can be thought of as a generalized version of the numeration systems studied by the mathematician Dumont. This characterization is presented in the form of a combinatorial interpretation, which in turn yields a statistical law governing the distribution of the order's contributing factors. This distribution is shown to be non-trivial and follows a gamma distribution when the system's parameters are finite, while it takes on a geometric distribution when the system is infinite. A theoretical framework known as weak lensing magnification influence on Type Ia supernovae (SNIa) is proposed as a potential tool to augment the observable universe with gravitational waves, specifically at high redshifts. This framework is tested using Pantheon data sets, with results indicating that the assumption of a linear relationship between SNIa flux and gravitational wave effects may not hold, as observed combinations of flux and lensing effects deviate from linearity by up to 3 sigma. This non-linearity could be a result of lensing by individual massive objects, and is found to be more pronounced for SNIa with longer observed wavelengths, a higher than expected peak magnitude, and in regions of the sky with higher than average foreground matter density. This effect may have significant implications for future SNIa surveys, particularly those that will be conducted with next-generation telescopes using new wavelength bands. This study also presents a method for detecting lensing effects on SNIa using Pantheon data, and suggests that a more sensitive survey with a magnitude limit of 2.5 Vega could potentially discover thousands of lensed SNIa in the near future. The efficiency and miniaturization of silicon photonic systems depend heavily on efficient light management within the T-shaped hub structure, which reduces loss and enables tighter spacing between photonic components. This T-shaped structure, also known as a T hub, can be utilized in various photonic elements including mode converters, beam splitters, and add-drop multiplexers. This article discusses the T hub structure's functionality, its effects on light behavior within the structure, and the implications for future silicon photonic design. We examine the T hub's parabolic and cusp-like features' effects on light and discuss strategies to minimize loss and optimize the design of this versatile photonic component. This article also presents numerical data on the T hub's performance in different configurations, which can be applied to various silicon photonic applications. This article targets an interdisciplinary audience of researchers and engineers working on silicon photonic systems, optical communication technology, and nanophotonics. This study focuses on a complex, inhomogeneous Kirchhoff type elliptic problem featuring the singular Trudenger-Moser inequality. We have obtained a new ground state solution for this problem under the conditions that the potential function is strictly sublinear, and a new pair of solutions for the related system, assuming one pair of conditions that includes a relationship between the growth rates of the potential functions. We also established the existence and multiplicity of solutions for this problem and its related system, respectively. These results build on previous work by Ambroso, Malchiodi, and Shahron, and the singular Trudenger-Moser inequality used is a recent variation proven by Ozsoge, Ryu, and Shanmugampillai. Additionally, we have explored the geomentric settings of this problem, specifically on compact Riemannian manifolds with boundary, and on the upper half-space $\mathbb{R}_+^n$. This has allowed us to obtain results for the corresponding systems in these geometric settings. This research also provides a new approach to the results of Li, Yang, and Zhao, and the work of Han, Lin, and Yang. We investigate the concentration behavior of sums of independent, identically distributed binary random variables with a specific negative correlation property. To achieve this, we establish upper bounds on the variance of these sums using a second moment, effectively generalizing a previous result from [Bandeira et al. 2016]. Furthermore, we analyze specific examples, including random permutations and Toeplitz matrices, to demonstrate how concentration disparities can be applied to gauge these examples' concentration behavior. Additionally, we explore an interesting connection between our approach and the log-Sobolev inequality, which enables us to obtain improved Poincaré constant estimates for certain Markov chains, such as the random permutation chain. Lastly, our approach yields an alternative proof of Bubin et al.'s [2019] result regarding the Gumbel distribution's concentration behavior. Given a closed symplectic manifold (M,ω) and a locally symplectic surface S in M, we define a symplectic modification of M as a specific type of symplectic transformation that maps S to a contact surface in M. This concept is equivalent to a particular kind of pseudo-holomorphic curve property for the surface S. We then identify conditions under which any symplectic filling of the contact structure defined by S is symplectically equivalent to a modification of the original manifold M. Specifically, if M has a certain property related to its pseudo-holomorphic curve behavior and if the surface S has a particular characteristic related to its symplectic area, then we can show that all fillings of the contact structure defined by S are symplectically equivalent to M. We also provide examples demonstrating that this property is not generally inherent to symplectically filled contact structures. Finally, we show that any open symplectic manifold can be viewed as a modification of the standard Euclidean space, and we establish a relationship between this property and the behavior of pseudo-holomorphic curves within it. This includes an examination of the conditions under which the filling of a closed curve by a pseudo-holomorphic curve is minimal, as well as an analysis of how these conditions change when we move from considering closed curves to homotopy classes of curves. We conclude by examining the connection between these results and a related concept called symplectic fillability, and we provide some related but as yet unresolved questions. The "ideal acceptance" concept, a key factor in kidney allocation, aims to balance the benefits of accepting a particular kidney transplant by weighing the patient's expected post-transplant survival against the expected survival of their potential future cross-antigen match recipients. To better understand this concept's implications, we examined how the ideal acceptance function affects patient allocation rankings. Our analysis shows that a common, commonly used function may lead to suboptimal outcomes by prioritizing patients based on their blood type rather than their medical needs. To address this issue, we suggest an alternative ideal acceptance function that accounts for the cross-antigen match risk distribution. By using a sample dataset from the United States, we found that this new function produces a more nuanced ranking of patients that is less influenced by their blood type. To assess its impact, we calculated the change in cumulative expected survival for all patients, finding that the new function results in significantly different rankings and, in turn, a different cumulative expected survival for many patients – an effect that varies by blood type. To gain further insights, we analyzed the cross-antigen match risks and ideal acceptance values for individual patients, revealing that the new function produces distinct outcomes for patients with different blood types, particularly those with type O. To improve patient allocation under the current system, we recommend adopting the new ideal acceptance function. To take it a step further, we suggest exploring alternative allocation strategies that prioritize the distribution of blood types among the transplant recipient population. To facilitate this research, we made the code used in this study publicly available. To address the limitations of this study, we recommend gathering more detailed data on the cross-antigen match risks and outcomes for individual patients. To this end, we proposed a potential data collection strategy that involves tracking the outcomes of all kidney transplant recipients in a single, large, diverse population. By doing so, we can gain a more nuanced understanding of the ideal acceptance concept and how it affects patient allocation and outcomes. Recent studies utilizing pre-trained language models to analyze the emotional content of words have shown promising results in several applications. Word representations that capture the polarity of words have been particularly effective in various tasks. However, the reliability of these representations has not been extensively tested, particularly under the framework proposed by Loughran and McDonald, which employs negative and positive word lists to gauge the emotional language used in company statements. In our research, we employed a wide array of word representations to classify words from the ISE (Institutional Shareholder Services) negative and positive lists and found that the accuracy rates vary widely, often falling short of 80%. Notably, the representations excel in identifying the most polar words but struggle with less intense polarities. Furthermore, we discovered that the models tend to conflate synonyms, even when those synonyms are not highly polar. Ultimately, our findings highlight the limitations of these representations and suggest that more nuanced methods may be necessary to capture the complexities of emotional language. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AmirGhafari/WordPolarity.

This paper presents single-input single-output orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (SISO-OFDM) and multi-input single-output orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (MISO-OFDM) formulations that enable fair comparison with the previously proposed Waveforming strategy. The SISO-OFDM formulation treats power allocation as a constant over time, while the MISO-OFDM formulation treats subcarrier allocation as a constant over time. The equivalence of these formulations to their respective Waveforming counterparts provides a clear and comparable benchmark for future research. Additionally, the paper highlights key observations regarding the optimal power allocation in SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM. The findings suggest that in scenarios with sufficient bandwidth, the optimal power allocation exhibits a "water-rising" behavior, whereas in scenarios with limited bandwidth, the optimal power allocation exhibits a "water-falling" behavior. The results demonstrate that an increase in the number of data subcarriers accelerates the "water-rising" or "water-falling" behavior. This method focuses on combining level-set and embedded boundary methods to address problems related to phase changes occurring at interfaces. By leveraging the strengths of both techniques, it enables the use of regularized $\delta$-functions with the EB method's flexibility, allowing for the treatment of moving boundaries within a Cartesian grid without the need for the creation of additional layers. This combined approach simplifies the computation of normal derivatives of the $\delta$-function, eliminating the need for finite difference approximations, and facilitates the efficient solution of problems involving the movement or disappearance of boundaries. This method has been successfully applied to solve problems related to solidification, melting, and freezing, as well as Stefan problems with Dirichlet boundary conditions, and has been implemented using a pseudo-spectral method that maintains high accuracy. Identifying rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer competitions can be challenging, especially when there are multiple players and strategies are partially observable. A key issue arises from the presence of unverifiable types of opponents, which can lead to an expansion of the strategy space and make it difficult to determine the set of all rationalizable equilibria. In a setting with private actions and type-verifiable payoffs, we develop an efficient method to enumerate the entire space of rationalizable equilibria using only the number of actions each player can take. This result holds true for generic payoff matrices and provides a significant improvement over previous approaches. Furthermore, our method allows for a characterization of the entire set of rationalizable equilibria, which can be useful for analyzing the impact of changing game parameters on this space. In addition, we show that this approach can be applied to a variety of special cases, including games with private actions and partially observable actions. In such cases, we can enumerate the set of rationalizable equilibria by conducting a local search around each Nash equilibrium. In the context of partially observable games, this can be further refined to focus on the set of weak strict equilibria. In the course of our analysis, we also explore connections with existing results on rationalizable behavior in one-shot games. A mathematical model of a spreading epidemic among individuals on a network is considered, where the network changes as infected individuals create new connections with each other. This model, based on the susceptible-infected-recovered dynamics, is used to examine how the epidemic spreads and eventually dies out. By applying a combination of analytical and numerical techniques to study this model's fundamental properties, researchers found that a critical threshold exists beyond which the epidemic ultimately declines. This threshold is influenced by various factors, including the rate at which new connections are formed and the size of the network. An important finding is that, in large networks, this critical threshold can be very close to one, which has significant implications for how effectively it can be increased through targeted interventions. This research also explored the distribution of time until the epidemic dies out and found that, in many cases, this distribution takes on a specific, long-lasting exponential form. An open question remains regarding the mechanism driving the rapid spread of the epidemic in its early stages. This model has been applied to a linear array of connections and revealed a surprising pattern of rapid epidemic spread through intermediate connections. This pattern is significant because it shows that removing the middle connections of a linear array can actually increase the rate at which the epidemic spreads through the array. To improve policy optimization efficiency, experience replay has been widely
utilized in model-free reinforcement learning methods by providing multiple
episodes of simulated data. However, the current approach simply combines
episodes randomly, which may not effectively utilize the variance of episodes
for enhanced policy optimization. A new experience replay method called VDER
is proposed in this paper, which dynamically adjusts the replay policy based
on the variance of episodes. VDER employs an exploration-exploitation
framework to adaptively balance the exploration of uncertain states and the
exploitation of certain states. The variance of episodes is calculated as a
measure of uncertainty, and a novel VDER algorithm is developed by
integrating the exploration-exploitation framework with the replay policy.
Theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate that VDER achieves a
faster policy optimization rate and a lower regret than the conventional
experience replay method. Experimental evaluations on multiple reinforcement
learning tasks confirm that VDER yields superior performance to conventional
experience replay methods. The code for VDER is publicly available online.

A key challenge in modified gravity theories is identifying their parameters that necessitate large-scale cosmological simulations, despite the fact that these simulations are now feasible for a wide array of models. To address this issue, a new method has been developed to efficiently conduct $N$-body simulations in altered gravity, using a simplified approach that focuses solely on the impact of these modifications on the distribution of galaxy masses and scales. This method, which relies on a set of modified gravity models based on conformally transformed dark matter, allows for rapid $N$-body simulations in altered gravity, even on modest computational resources. To demonstrate this approach's capabilities, a range of altered gravity simulations have been performed, including three new models, and the resulting galaxy distributions have been compared to their standard $\Lambda$CDM counterparts. These comparisons reveal the altered gravity effects on galaxy distributions and provide a foundation for using these simulations in altered gravity in combination with semi-analytical galaxy formation models. These models, which simulate galaxy formation based on the properties of dark matter halos, can then be used to identify the altered gravity parameters that best match the observed galaxy populations. These simulations are now available for public use through the website of the GravDynE collaboration.

MediaWiki platforms, as seen with Wikipedia, have a strong track record of facilitating collaborative projects. By leveraging the existing infrastructure of Wikipedia, the WorkingWiki project aims to create a flexible environment for interconnecting and combining multiple research projects. This endeavor, initiated in 2010, has already successfully integrated several research initiatives, including the BioWiki Challenge, where participants were tasked with inferring protein functions based on annotated Wikipedia pages, and the WikiGene prediction contest. A key feature of WorkingWiki is its ability to manage and analyze large datasets associated with Wikipedia pages, offering a versatile tool for exploring various research projects. With its modular design, the platform can be easily adapted to accommodate diverse research settings, making WorkingWiki an accessible platform for an expansive range of collaborative studies. As evidence of its utility, the paper presents empirical assessments of WorkingWiki's performance in two research contexts. By leveraging the capabilities of Wikipedia and the flexibility of its underlying infrastructure, WorkingWiki serves as a prime example of how collaborative research can be effectively conducted using MediaWiki platforms. The integration of functional genomics data with genome-wide association study (GWAS) results is a well-established approach to pinpointing the precise genes and regions responsible for associations between genetic variation and traits or diseases. As a significant advancement in this field, the ENCODE project's comprehensive identification of functional elements across the genome has created new opportunities for analysis. In response, we developed a method for assessing the relationship between functional elements and associations between genetic variation and traits or diseases. Utilizing a combination of position-based and expression-based approaches, we examined the relationship between 18 different traits or diseases and various functional elements across the genome. Our findings reveal that certain regions of the genome associated with certain traits or diseases tend to be linked to specific biological processes, and that certain types of functional elements are more frequently involved in these associations than others. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the disparities in regional associations across different tissues and cells, as well as the variability in associations for different types of functional elements. By exploring these disparities and variations, we gained a more nuanced understanding of the regional and element-level characteristics of the genome associated with different traits or diseases. Our approach and findings are applicable to a broad range of research questions and provide a foundation for the analysis of current and future functional genomics data. Our methodology, along with our results for the 18 human characteristics studied here, are available online at http://genenetwork.nl/gdview. Our study demonstrates the value of integrating functional genomics data with GWAS results and highlights the potential of this approach for guiding experimental design and prioritizing targets for experimental validation. Our findings also underscore the significance of considering the cellular context in which associations between genetic variation and traits or diseases occur, and the importance of accounting for the diversity of functional elements across different cell types and tissues. Our research suggests that a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships between genetic variation and traits or diseases requires the integration of multiple sources of data, including functional genomics data from different cell types and tissues, and highlights the need for a more inclusive and integrative approach to studying the genomics of complex traits. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has been highly effective in discovering a wide array of short-lived, elementary particles, both new and rare decay modes of established particles. Despite its limited size and energy, the LHC has achieved a broad reach in mass ranges, from just a few GeV to over a TeV, thanks to its powerful collision capabilities. This article reviews the various "Tiny Systems" studied in recent years at the LHC, encompassing three main categories of physics: Higgs boson properties in tiny systems, studies of the strong force in tiny systems, and searches for dark matter in the form of faint signals from tiny systems. Each of these areas has produced significant findings that have advanced our understanding of the fundamental forces of nature, the behavior of matter at its most basic level, and the composition of the universe. This review summarizes the latest discoveries from the LHC, highlighting the significance of its research and the importance of its continued operation. With its ongoing upgrades and expansion to even higher energy levels, the LHC will undoubtedly reveal even more of the universe's hidden secrets in the years to come. Observations of some neutron star low-mass X-ray binary transients have revealed that their outbursts often follow a pattern with progressively longer intervals between successive bursts. A key feature of these binaries is the rate at which their outburst intervals increase, typically measured over two bursts. This rate can be either positive, indicating that the binaries will eventually move to outbursts with longer periods than typically observed, or negative, suggesting they may eventually move to outbursts with periods that are typically considered superoutburst or recurrent nova-like. Utilizing a new method that compares outburst periods to their square roots, we found that the outburst intervals of GSXDE J173725-27393 and CXO J165835.0-525626 are characterized by negative rates, making them the first two known examples of this type. This feature is now a part of the diversity of outburst patterns observed in this binary class. Furthermore, we found that the outburst intervals of the recently discovered X-ray transient Gaia J044794.9-630338, likely a low-mass neutron star binary, also exhibit a negative rate, suggesting it may contain either a neutron star or a white dwarf primary. This finding is particularly significant for the latter case as it would be the first low-mass X-ray binary with a negative outburst period index and also the first with an estimated primary mass below 1.2 solar masses. This discovery is also notable for the Galactic Centre, where this binary's outburst pattern, combined with its optical and near-infrared colours, supports the hypothesis that some low-luminosity X-ray transient populations in the Galactic Centre may be characterized by transient outbursts rather than persistent X-ray emission. This is further reinforced by the discovery of a new transient in the Galactic Centre with a low-mass primary and a long outburst recurrence time. This new transient, Gaia J174514.9-281449, which is likely a low-mass X-ray binary, has a low X-ray luminosity and is associated with a 2.5 solar mass companion in a short orbital period. This discovery suggests that low-mass X-ray binaries with low-mass primaries may have a broader range of orbital periods than previously thought and that some of these binaries may have long outburst recurrence times, potentially similar to those of recurrent novae. The rapid development of time and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-ARPES) has enabled the visualization of light-dependent modifications to energy and momentum distributions of one-electron states in molecules and solids. In this work, we outline the fundamental principles of TR-ARPES and discuss various light-induced effects seen in non-rigid molecular frameworks, as well as in localized and delocalized electrons within solids. This review also delves into the distinct characteristics of electron and nuclear motion, and discusses the implications of spin-vibrational interactions on various phenomena. Furthermore, we discuss theoretical approaches to modeling light-induced electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational interactions, and highlight the significance of these interactions in chemical reactions, optical properties, and the thermal and optical conductivity of solids. By integrating TR-ARPES with other experimental techniques and theoretical frameworks, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of light-induced interactions and their effects on the dynamics of solids and molecules. This review also highlights the potential of TR-ARPES in driving advances in solid-state theory, molecular chemistry, and materials science. This review is intended for graduate students and researchers in the fields of chemistry, physics, and materials science. Understanding the semantics of sentences within a discourse context is a complex task that involves grasping not just individual meanings, but also the relationships between them. To measure this comprehension, we employ Natural Language Inference (NLI), which assesses the logical connections between sentences. In a typical NLI task, two sentences with a designated logical connection are provided, but in the discourse context case, only two sentences are given without a specified relation. We investigate how different NLI relations affect the discourse context interpretation and use a pre-trained language model to extract semantic features from the sentences. These features are then used in a selection mechanism that determines the most suitable NLI relation, effectively a variety of semantic combinations. We find that the most prevalent NLI relation in discourse contexts is "entailment" followed by a significant gap before the next most common, with neural network-based features successfully capturing this variety. This is further supported by a simpler feature extraction method that also reveals the same semantic variety pattern. Within this structure, the radiative dynamics of afterglows is characterized by four distinct phases, influenced by various physical processes including radiative and adiabatic dynamics, interaction with the surrounding medium, and the effects of magnetic fields and Comptonization. Re-deriving key equations using a simple, intuitive approach, we provide explicit expressions for radiative phases, from the initial burst through to the persistent phase, with examples of how the various phases intersect. We establish the equivalence of two definitions for a function field in characteristic p > 0 to have a relative trace map that is compatible with the Frobenius-Schwarz reflection property. This compatibility is expressed through the residual arithmetic of the function field. Next, we show that over a finite extension of the rational numbers, a function field of genus 0 and specified absolute Galois group has a relative trace map that is compatible with the Frobenius-Schwarz reflection property if and only if its algebraic closure is residually Galois and possesses a complete residue map. Finally, we demonstrate that in the case of genus 0, a field that is residually Galois and possesses a complete residue map can be considered as the function field of a smooth curve over the rational numbers, although this result is not generic when the absolute Galois group is an arbitrary linear group. Additionally, we provide an alternative proof of a key result from Harvey's work. Lastly, we examine the relationship between the absolute and relative absolute Galois groups of such fields.

Notably, when we consider the order three iteration of the Euler-Poincaré 1-cocycle, it takes on a particular form that can be linked to the Vassiliev invariant known as the Bracken-Weinstein invariant, making this the first instance where a Vassiliev invariant of order three is generated through a cocycle. In a federated learning setup, institutions collaborate to train a model by
exchanging parameters while maintaining individual student data private. However, we
demonstrate that an attacker, positioned within the learning federation and
motivated by a desire to compromise student privacy, can design carefully
crafted attacks to access sensitive information about individual students. We
introduce two such attacks - a privacy-invasive assault that uncovers a student's
identity or a privacy-disclosure assault that uncovers a student's sensitive
attribute - and illustrate the effectiveness of these attacks using real data
sets from institutions such as Stanford and a synthetic dataset mimicking a
large-scale real-world setting. We further investigate various factors that
influence the efficacy of these attacks and possible countermeasures that
institutions can employ to safeguard their students' privacy within a federated
learning framework. We open-source our code and data generation tools at: \url{https://github.com/PragmaticAttack/PAtool}. Deep kernel methods have shown superior performance in various tasks by efficiently leveraging high dimensional data with linear scalability. Although these methods facilitate the incorporation of diverse kernel functions with inherent properties, such as positive definiteness, they often rely on pre-computed kernel matrices, which can be cumbersome to select and may not effectively capture the underlying structure of the data. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework for kernel estimation in high-dimensional spaces by utilizing random Fourier attributes of the input data. This approach yields a data-dependent kernel estimator that is computationally efficient and exhibits linear scalability with respect to data dimensions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method by incorporating it into a stochastic kernel support vector machine framework, which outperforms the traditional SVM with pre-computed kernel in various experiments. The proposed kernel estimator is also found to be a compact representation of the data that preserves its intrinsic structure, as evident from its ability to accurately reconstruct the input data. The code for our proposed method is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ashwin-ml/FourierKernelEstimation}.

Our research introduces an innovative approach called the Cartesian Decomposition Method for embedding groups into Garland products. This method provides a structured representation of groups as product representations, offering a clear depiction of their underlying structure. We demonstrate how this approach can be applied to effectively analyze and visualize specific types of groups, specifically those with distinct subgroup properties. Furthermore, we show that this method can be utilized to identify specific subgroups within product groups, including the embedded form of well-known groups such as dihedral and symmetric groups. Our approach can be tailored to accommodate various types of groups by adjusting the structure of our product arrays. We also propose a graphical framework for constructing product arrays based on the relationships between subgroups and their corresponding embedded forms. Our research offers a versatile tool for exploring the intricacies of group structures and provides a valuable resource for educators seeking engaging visualizations of group concepts. We believe this approach has significant potential for further applications in group theory beyond the scope of this paper. Our research is complemented by an accompanying webpage containing interactive visualizations of the groups examined in this study. Each stream is trained on its own, yet they share a common set of features, allowing them to be fused into a unified model. The accuracy of hand-counted election ballot results relies heavily on the precise interpretation of optically scanned symbols. Research suggests that even small errors in this process can significantly impact the reliability of election outcomes. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called Informed Optical Symbol Recognition (iOCR). This method utilizes a combination of machine learning techniques to create a customized symbol recognition system that learns from the patterns of actual count data. Through simulations and real-world testing with Australian ballot samples, iOCR demonstrated improved accuracy compared to leading commercial OCR solutions, with an average error rate approximately 2.5 times lower. In one notable instance, iOCR correctly identified an error in a ballot count that a human reviewer had also missed, highlighting the potential benefits of this approach for detecting and correcting data entry mistakes during the counting process. By providing a more precise and informed method for interpreting scanned symbols, iOCR offers an accessible solution for reducing errors in hand-counted election ballot results. In recent years, over-parametrized linear models have gained significant attention, offering both computationally efficient and high-performing solutions for various statistical tasks. However, beyond theoretical results, the practical significance of over-parametrization in real-world applications, particularly within linear regression for time series data, has not been thoroughly explored. This paper delves into the study of over-parametrized linear regression for time series by analyzing the conditions under which additional parameters do not lead to performance degradation, a phenomenon we term as "benign misfitting." Our findings reveal that the absence of degradation (a "benign" scenario) is guaranteed when the number of parameters does not exceed the time series length, under certain norm constraints on the data and weights. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in cases where the data exhibits complex structures and high dimensionalities, there are specific conditions under which the absence of degradation holds true. Our results also provide a framework for understanding the effects of over-parametrization in time series regression within the "benign misfitting" framework. A key challenge in using self-planning for optimal energy management in decentralized markets involves managing storage effectively. While storage can be both a supplier and a consumer of energy, deciding when to charge or discharge it requires consideration of future prices to avoid selling at low prices or buying at high ones. This approach ensures that future prices within these intervals will result in prices either above the selling price or below the buying price. By limiting the scope of possible prices, a subset of future prices is considered safe, allowing for decision-making about charging, discharging, or doing nothing. This approach is tested on real-world data from Germany, demonstrating the benefits of cautious self-planning. The results reveal that the proportion of safe prices varies significantly over time and is influenced by seasonal patterns, leading to an annual change of 20%. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of considering multiple days of data when determining the optimal time to charge or discharge energy. The development of the cutoff-based self-planning approach provides a foundation for further research into more advanced methods of predicting future prices. A range of circulation regimes emerge, including geostrophic circulation on thick atmospheres of rapidly rotating planets, cyclostrophic circulation on thin atmospheres of rapidly rotating planets, and super-rotation on thin atmospheres of slowly rotating planets. A regime of turbulent circulation is found on thin atmospheres of gas giants with low viscosity. To advance this effort, a theoretical framework based on a new multi-valley effective weight theory has been developed to accurately predict the behavior of up to four donors in a [111] direction. This model goes beyond previous approximations by effectively capturing the influence of valley mixing on the electronic properties. Using a CI framework, simulations of donor pairs showed that the inclusion of valley mixing is crucial, particularly in modifying the energy separation between different spin configurations. Furthermore, in a triple donor, the inclusion of valley mixing was found to be essential for correctly identifying the ground state spin configuration. This theoretical framework has been validated by comparing the results to experimental measurements and can be utilized to guide the realization of specific quantum simulations, such as implementing a Kitaev model or creating a connection to a Hubbard model, by adjusting the amount of valley mixing and donor-atom bonding. This is achievable through variations in the donor-atom chemical bond and implantation direction. This development is expected to facilitate the exploration of various quantum phenomena in silicon-based quantum simulations. This approach has been implemented using a publicly available code. Research advances in quantum materials and surface science have led to the discovery of unique two-dimensional semiconductors with controllable band structures and interfaces. This class of materials enables the creation of complex geometries with diverse electronic properties, offering opportunities to explore exotic phenomena in one dimension. Here, a novel three-dimensional structure consisting of HgTe quantum trenches without energy gaps is proposed, with a one-dimensional interface between a semiconducting (100) HgTe surface and a (111)A HgTe surface that exhibits massless Dirac electrons. By developing a theoretical model, the transport properties of this one-dimensional interface are investigated under various trench configurations. Results show that the interplay between the trench width and height can create diverse one-dimensional scattering scenarios, from ballistic transport to the formation of one-dimensional helical magnetic gaps along the interface. This breakthrough paves the way for exploring one-dimensional physics in a controlled setting, with the ability to design unique transport properties in the HgTe (111)A surface. This finding also highlights the versatility of HgTe surfaces as a material platform for quantum transport research. This study is followed by Chapter 7, where this structure is modified to create a one-dimensional interface between a semiconducting (100) HgTe surface and a (111)B HgTe surface that exhibits massive Dirac electrons. This will be referred to as a HgTe quantum wire. This chapter focuses on the transport properties of a single HgTe quantum wire with a very small width, and discusses the role of boundary roughness on the wave function of the wire. This will be further explored in Chapter 7. This research was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. To ensure efficient and reliable data transmission in 5G networks using Time Division Duplexing technology, a new approach called Dynamic TDD has been proposed. This method allows for the reallocation of uplink and downlink transmission periods in response to changing network conditions. To manage this process, a new architectural component called Model Allocation Services was introduced, which utilizes predictive models to guide reallocation decisions. However, the increased computational requirements for these models necessitate a more efficient allocation strategy. A recent research effort addressed this challenge by developing an efficient method for selecting a subset of models to support Dynamic TDD. In a simulation study using a representative 5G system architecture, this approach was found to reduce computational costs by 2.5 times while maintaining similar performance to the original approach. A subsequent investigation into an alternative implementation showed that this efficiency gain could be further increased to 4.5 times with only a minor performance degradation. A subsequent issue with model drift, which results in predictive models becoming outdated due to changing network conditions, was also examined. A solution to this problem was found by implementing a simple update mechanism that reduces the duration of model drift from 100 seconds to just 20 seconds. A subsequent game-theoretic approach was developed to manage model allocation in Dynamic TDD networks. This approach, which accounts for differences in model accuracy and the costs associated with model updates, was found to result in an equilibrium state that maximizes overall network performance. A simulation study confirmed the effectiveness of this approach in networks with varying numbers of base stations and under different network conditions. It also showed that this approach can handle large numbers of base stations and is resilient in the face of interference and cell loading. A further examination into the challenges of implementing Dynamic TDD in practice identified the difficulty of synchronizing the reallocation of transmission periods across different base stations. This issue was addressed by developing a distributed algorithm that allows for independent reallocation decisions across different base stations. Recent studies suggest that optimizing over a carefully selected set of models can provide an estimation of gradients, which has been successfully applied in various settings such as adversarial attacks and resource allocation. Building upon this concept, we explore the potential of using Hamiltonian Neural Networks to derive gradients, examining both theoretical limitations and practical applications through simulated and real-world examples. In particular, we investigate the relationship between the chosen hyperparameter, effective learning rate, and an intuitive analog of generalization error. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of NTK-based models in solving a simple linear regression problem and showcase the effectiveness of our gradient estimation in a more complex setting using the CIFAR-10 dataset. Lastly, we discuss potential improvements, including the optimization of a single model and the connection to effective learning rate, and explore an unexplored scenario of estimating the eigenvector of the NTK matrix. All code is available at https://github.com/zhengqi-liu/hamiltonian-gradients.

The growing need to deploy artificial intelligence quickly and efficiently has led to a surge in the use of pre-trained models without rigorous testing, which can result in compromised safety and reliability in critical applications. This issue is particularly pronounced in new domains where data is scarce, leading to a reliability crisis that necessitates immediate intervention. To address this challenge, we present a novel collaborative method called "ScoreAndSelect" that involves a dynamic team of multiple agents, including a machine learning model, using a combination of model-based performance assessments and strategic decision-making to maximize reliability. The method allows for seamless integration of new data and model performance feedback, which are used to update the model and domain knowledge. A robust trust-rating system is introduced to evaluate the performance of individual agents and data contributions, enabling selective inclusion of high-performing agents and valuable data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ScoreAndSelect through experiments on critical transportation applications, showcasing a significant improvement in the accuracy of the selected model and a substantial increase in the diversity of the chosen data. The efficiency and efficacy of ScoreAndSelect are further highlighted by comparing it with alternative baselines. The code for ScoreAndSelect is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/IBM/ScoreAndSelect. Experimental data and models are available at https://coclub.org/projects/scoreselect. Or you can contact the corresponding author at [liang@cs.wisc.edu](liang@cs.wisc.edu).

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) aims to identify the appropriate sense of a word with multiple senses based on its context.  Despite significant advances in natural language processing, current pre-trained language models have not significantly improved WSD performance.  To address this, we propose a strategy to enhance the effectiveness of BERT for WSD by utilizing two types of context: background knowledge and instance-specific context.  Background knowledge encompasses general information about a word's senses, whereas instance-specific context pertains to the unique details of a particular text.  We extract relevant knowledge from the context, known as glosses, which we incorporate into the input for a BERT-based model.  To selectively utilize instance-specific context, we employ a score that represents each sense's relevance to the context.  By selecting the sense with the highest score, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on three popular WSD benchmarks.  When combining our approach with a strong BERT-based model, the results show a significant improvement of 4.63% on the average F-score.  Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-li/ContextGlossEnhancement.  Our findings suggest that effective WSD relies on a deeper understanding of the context, which can be achieved by leveraging both background knowledge and instance-specific context.  To facilitate this, we propose a simple yet effective strategy to utilize the context for WSD.  Our approach is versatile and can be applied to other BERT-based models by integrating the context into the input. In 1982, CERN's Intersecting Storage Rings began colliding protons with ammonia nitrogen (NH3) nuclei at an energy of 24.03 GeV. Using this data, we developed an algorithm to identify the sources of top quark pairs based on events containing a missing jet and two energetic jets. Approximately 0.2 nanobarns of data were collected, which is insufficient to detect top quarks directly. However, by applying the algorithm to simulated top quark and W boson events, we were able to establish a threshold for producing the equivalent of 10,000 top quark pairs at an energy of 541 GeV using a proton-proton collider. This achievement allows us to extend the algorithm to other colliding experiments, such as those involving antiprotons and heavy nuclei. The detection of top quark generation in these experiments will require significantly larger integrated luminosities. For example, an energy of 541 GeV in the ISR required an integrated luminosity of at least 10 nanobarns, which is equivalent to 10 times the initial integrated luminosity achieved in this experiment. This is comparable to the integrated luminosities reached in later experiments at the same energy, such as the Tevatron proton-antiproton collider at an energy of 1.8 TeV. This optimization will be crucial for detecting top quark generation in future experiments, such as the LHC proton-proton and heavy ion colliders. Thanks to advances in natural language processing, generating code from natural language descriptions has significantly improved. However, code generation in complex systems like databases with strict schema requirements poses a major challenge. A new approach called CodeGen has been proposed to tackle this issue by directly generating SQL from raw text. While effective, CodeGen struggles with several limitations. Firstly, it relies on a pre-trained language model with a vast amount of data, making it resource-intensive. Secondly, it requires a massive dataset of labeled text and SQL code, which is difficult to obtain. Lastly, CodeGen struggles with adapting to new domains with limited data. To address these constraints, a new method called CDT has been introduced. CDT is a dual-process framework that separates text analysis from code generation. It employs a retrieval-based approach to extract relevant information from text and a conditional generation method to produce code. The effectiveness of CDT has been demonstrated across multiple domains with varying levels of data availability. Results show that CDT outperforms CodeGen in all domains tested. To further improve performance, CDT has been applied to a previously untested domain with promising outcomes. The code for CDT has been made publicly available. All data used in this research is real-world and has been sourced from the WebTable dataset except for the new domain, which was sourced from the TREC WebTable Track. All experiments have been conducted on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. All data and models have been made publicly available on GitHub. The performance of CDT has been compared to CodeGen, DBPARSER, TTRQL, TSQLDUAL, and SQLFlow. The reference and each modeled text contain the same set of letters. The letter frequencies in the modeled texts converge to the letter frequencies in the reference as their length increases. The extensive deviation principles for empirical letter frequencies in these modeled texts are examined and explicit bounds are derived. Specifically, an entropy-like quantity is defined as the sum of the Shannon entropies for each letter's frequency distribution across all modeled texts. The entropy-like quantity provides an indication of how significantly the modeled texts deviate from the reference. In this context, we prove that any surface $\Sigma$ that is a local minimum within a homotopy class of maps from $\Sigma$ to $\mathbb{M}$, can be obtained through a variation of its area functional. Additionally, we demonstrate that if $\mathbb{M}$ has a finite volume, then the set of all surfaces within a homotopy class of maps from $\Sigma$ to $\mathbb{M}$ that are local minima, is compact according to the $H^1$-topology. Furthermore, we show that for a surface $\Sigma$ with a boundary, the corresponding category $\text{cat}_{\Sigma,\partial \Sigma}(\mathbb{M})$ can be defined and is equivalent to the category $\text{cat}_\Sigma(\mathbb{M})$. Lastly, we establish an inequality relating the area of a surface that is a local minimum within a homotopy class of maps from $\Sigma$ to $\mathbb{M}$, to the volume of $\mathbb{M}$, with a specific bound depending on the genus of $\Sigma$ and its intrinsic curvature. This inequality can be seen as a variant of the well-known volume comparison theorem of Gromov-Lawrence-Sidorov-Thomson, with an improvement in its constants. A theoretical model involving a tensor monopole interaction is proposed, which predicts that 64Ni will exhibit coexistence of superconducting and normal states for zero spin. This prediction aligns with experimental findings indicating a mixture of 0+ and 2+ excited states at low energy, likely resulting from the coexistence of superconducting and normal components. By incorporating a BCS framework and considering the neutron-proton asymmetry in 64Ni, the model successfully explains the observed magnetic quadrupole moments of the 0+ and 2+ states. It also predicts that the most superconducting component will occupy a specific Nilsson configuration, allowing for the identification of key states and facilitating analysis of inelastic scattering off 64Ni. Notably, this model highlights the importance of the tensor monopole interaction in neutron-rich nuclei, particularly its significant impact on magnetic properties, which may otherwise be misattributed to other effects. Machine learning models often require feature scaling to prevent certain features from dominating others.  However, the impact of this transformation on model performance depends on multiple factors including the dataset, task type, and evaluation metric.  To account for these variations, the range of feature values is commonly standardized using mean and standard deviation.  An alternative method involves scaling based on interquartile range (IQR), which has been found to be beneficial for some datasets.  However, both methods share a significant shortcoming - they treat all data points equally, which can lead to an uneven representation of extreme cases in the model.  This issue is particularly pronounced in NLP, where the influence of all data points can vary significantly due to the presence of word frequencies.  This paper delves into the effects of standard scaling on word frequencies and explores alternative methods of scaling, which can mitigate the bias in models.  Specifically, we investigate the effect of standard scaling on word frequencies and the resulting models, and demonstrate that a particular form of k-fold jackknife cross-validation can significantly reduce the variance of models when compared to traditional scaling methods.  This reduction in variance is shown to be particularly pronounced when models are trained on datasets with a high frequency of rare words.  This finding is illustrated through the analysis of two NLP datasets, specifically the 20 Newgroups and IMDB sentiment analysis datasets.  This paper also discusses the implications of these findings for model selection and hyperparameter tuning.  Overall, our research highlights the importance of considering the distribution of data frequencies when evaluating models, and the benefits of using k-fold jackknife cross-validation to reduce variance in model evaluation.  This reduction in variance can be observed in both the standard scaling of features and the selection of hyperparameters.  This paper also presents a tool for scaling features and evaluating models using k-fold jackknife cross-validation, which is available for public use.  This tool allows users to select from multiple scaling methods, including standard scaling based on mean and standard deviation, IQR scaling, and minimum-maximum scaling.  This tool can be used to train and evaluate models using k-fold jackknife cross-validation, and also provides a function for plotting the distribution of word frequencies in a given dataset.  This tool is particularly useful for researchers and practitioners in the field of NLP, where the distribution of word frequencies can significantly impact model performance.  This paper also presents a case study on the effect of standard scaling on word frequencies in the context of a specific NLP task, specifically the classification of medical entities.

Our study examines the significance of elliptical flow in small systems of Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, utilizing data from the STAR and PHOBOS experiments and comparing it with predictions from transport and hydrodynamic models. We focus on triangular flow $v_3$ in these systems, obtained through the 4-particle cumulant correlation analysis. Our results show that $v_3$ values derived from different methods are consistent and similar across transport and hydrodynamic models, indicating that initial eccentricities are responsible for elliptical flow. Furthermore, our findings suggest that elliptical flow is independent of collision energy but scales with the geometric property of the system, contradicting expectations based on hydrodynamic models that predict an increase in elliptical flow with rising energy. We also investigate the internal structure of the system that drives elliptical flow and find that it is influenced by the initial eccentricity of the system rather than its internal geometry. Our analysis of the relationship between the size of the system's initial eccentricity and its internal geometry may be explained by a model in which the initial eccentricity of the system is independent of its geometric properties. We propose that this model could be a fundamental property of the system's initial state and that it may be a critical factor in driving the transition from elliptical to triangular flow in small systems of Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions.
